en: The Legend of the Elder Sumaṅgala The Lion-Throne Chapter, Number Ten I was a king named Mahāpanāda, ruling over the earth. At that time, the Teacher, the Blessed One, appeared in the world. He was the Buddha Kassapa, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened One. Having brought the fourfold assembly to maturity, he passed away into Nibbāna. His relics were distributed throughout Jambudīpa. A stūpa was erected for him at the city of Kusinārā. It was a magnificent structure, adorned with a parasol and a pinnacle. I had a son named Sumaṅgala, who was wise and possessed of great splendor. He was handsome, virtuous, and beloved by the people. He went to that stūpa of the Buddha Kassapa, and having circumambulated it three times, he offered a lion-throne. With a mind full of faith, he made this aspiration: "May I, through this root of merit, become a Buddha in the future. Through that deed, I have attained the state of a Buddha. I am the Buddha Gotama, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened One. By means of that very same deed, I have reached the goal. I have crossed over the ocean of saṃsāra; there is no further rebirth for me. This is my final birth; I shall not be born again. Thus, by the power of that gift of a lion-throne, I have attained the supreme state of Buddhahood. Therefore, one should offer a lion-throne to the stūpa of a Buddha, for such a deed brings about the attainment of Buddhahood. Thus ends the legend of the Elder Sumaṅgala.
“Desiring to offer a sacrifice,
having prepared the food,
I was waiting upon the brahmins.”
Standing on a spacious terrace,
I saw the Perfectly Enlightened One,
lovely to behold and of great renown.
To the Guide of the entire world,
the Self-Existent One, the Supreme Person,
the Blessed One, the Radiant One.
Honored by his disciples,
shining like the sun as he proceeded along the highway.
Raising my hands in reverential salutation,
I gladdened my own heart;
with my mind alone, I invited him.
"Let the Great Sage come.
Perceiving my intention,
the Teacher, unsurpassed in the world, [arrived].
Accompanied by a thousand whose taints were destroyed,
he approached my door.
Homage to you, O noble steed among men!
Homage to you, O Supreme among Men;
having ascended the palace,
please sit upon the lion throne.
Tamed, with a tamed retinue,
crossed over, the best among those who ferry others across;
having ascended the palace,
He sat upon the excellent seat.
Whatever food was available in my own home, I presented it [to him].
With a confident heart and a joyful mind, I gave it to the Buddha with my own hands out of faith.
Born of the Vedas, with palms joined in reverence,
I pay homage to the Supreme Buddha; oh,
how sublime is the Buddha’s excellence!
While eight [of us] were attending upon you,
many whose taints were destroyed partook [of food];
this is indeed your power, Ānanda.
To him I go for refuge.
And the Blessed One Piyadassī,
the Eldest in the World, the Bull among Men;
Having sat down in the community of monks,
he spoke these verses:
"He who fed the Saṅgha..."
Listen as I speak of the Tathāgata, the perfectly awakened one, who has become upright and concentrated.
Twenty-seven times he will exercise sovereignty over the gods;
delighted by his own deeds, he—
He will delight in the world of the gods.
Ten and eight times he will become a wheel-turning monarch.
‘He shall rule the earth for five hundred years,
dwelling upon the land after having seized the wilderness forests.
Having entered the forest wilds,
In the forest frequented by tigers,
having exerted myself in striving,
my defilements have been incinerated.
In eighteen hundred kappas,
because of the gift I gave then,
I have not known a miserable rebirth.
This is the fruit of giving alms-food:
the four analytical knowledges and these eight liberations.
"The six direct knowledges have been realized;
the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Thus indeed did the venerable elder Sumaṅgala speak these verses.
The legend of the Elder Sumaṅgala is the tenth.
Its summary verse:
Sīhāsanī and Ekathambhī...
And Nanda and Cūḷapanthaka;
Pilindavaccha, Rāhula, Vaṅganta, and Raṭṭhapāla.
The Sopāka and the Maṅgala,
ten in the second chapter;
and one hundred and thirty-eight.
And here a verse has been proclaimed.
The second chapter, the Sīhāsaniya-vagga.
